newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavarian minister Huber backs Waigel on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Bavarian minister Huber backs Waigel on EMU.

text.p: A key political ally from Finance Minister Theo Waigel's home state of Bavaria said on Monday that Germany must meet the Maastricht treaty's strict borrowing target if European monetary union is to start on schedule.

Bavarian Finance Minister Erwin Huber, of the Christian Social Union (CSU), also dismissed calls for party leader Waigel to resign over his handling of Bonn's budget crisis, saying he did not know of anyone who could do the job better.

Huber, in an interview with German Radio, restated his party's line that Bonn must cut the budget deficit this year to at most 3.0 percent of gross domestic product for the CSU to support starting the single currency as planned in 1999.
"We have for five years said that the euro can only start if it is as strong as the mark," Huber said. "How can we guarantee stability to our citizens if we fudge the first important decision?"
Waigel's CSU is the Bavarian sister party to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), which together rule in coalition with the pro-business Free Democrats (FDP).

Huber dismissed charges the CSU was indulging in 'criteria fetishism', and added it was possible to meet the deficit goal this year without raising taxes if bold savings are made at all levels of government. The FDP has refused to back tax hikes.

Waigel, the longest-serving German finance minister since World War Two, has come in for devastating criticism over his failed bid to revalue the Bundesbank's gold reserves to help balance his budget sums this year.
But Huber said the CSU, including eurosceptic Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber, stood four-square behind Waigel.
"I don't know anyone who could do the job better," Huber said, adding he was convinced Waigel would win re-election as party leader at the CSU party conference next November.

Huber also said he was not aware of the details of a meeting between Waigel and former Social Democrat Chancellor Helmut Schmidt which news reports said had sounded out the possibility of creating a left-right "grand coalition" to replace Kohl's strained 14-year-old ruling alliance.
